tasks.title: Node NotReady: kubelet stopped
tasks.question:
ssh cka01001
The worker node node01 is reported as NotReady. Investigate the cause and bring node01 back to the Ready state. Your fix must survive a reboot of node01.
keys: fix must survive reboot (enable the service)
tasks.setup:
ssh node01 'systemctl stop kubelet; systemctl disable kubelet' 2>/dev/null
sleep 60
clear

steps.title: See which node is sick
steps.why: NotReady usually means the kubelet on that node is not talking. If it still says Ready, wait 30 s and run it again. The control plane waits ~50 s before marking a node NotReady.

steps.title: Log in to node01 and become root
steps.why: The kubelet runs on the node itself, not as a pod. systemctl changes need root. The real exam requires sudo -i. Killercoda is already root, so it changes nothing there.

steps.title: Check the kubelet service
steps.why: Shows the kubelet is stopped and will not start at boot.

steps.title: Start it and enable it at boot
steps.why: enable = survives reboot, --now = start right away.

steps.title: Go back and check
steps.why: Two exits: one leaves root, one leaves node01. Wait up to 30s for the node to report Ready.

tasks.beginner: The kubelet on node01 is switched off; turn it on and make it start automatically. Words you need: kubelet = the node agent that starts pods and reports to the control plane; NotReady = the control plane stopped hearing from that kubelet; systemctl enable = start the service at every boot.

tasks.title: Service has no endpoints
tasks.question:
ssh cka01002
In namespace shop the Service cart does not forward traffic to the Pods of Deployment cart. Fix the Service so that it routes to the Deployment's Pods. Do not modify the Deployment.
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace shop --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: cart, namespace: shop}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: cart}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: cart}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - {name: nginx, image: nginx:1.27-alpine, ports: [{containerPort: 80}]}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: cart, namespace: shop}
spec:
  selector: {app: carts}
  ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 80}]
EOF
clear

steps.title: See the empty endpoints
steps.see:
NAME          ADDRESSTYPE   PORTS   ENDPOINTS   AGE
cart-xxxxx    IPv4          80      <unset>     1m
steps.why: ENDPOINTS <unset> = no Pod IPs: the Service selector matches no Pod.

steps.title: Compare labels and selector
cmds: kubectl -n shop get svc cart -o wide
steps.why: One letter typo in the selector.

steps.title: Fix the selector
steps.why: Point the Service at the real Pod label.

steps.title: Test from inside the cluster
cmds: kubectl -n shop run tmp --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- -T3 cart
steps.why: A real request proves traffic flows.

tasks.beginner: The Service is looking for the wrong Pod label; correct its selector. Words you need: label = a name tag on a Pod (app=cart); selector = the label a Service looks for; EndpointSlice = the list of Pod IPs the Service found.

tasks.title: Pods stuck Pending (requests too big)
tasks.question:
ssh cka01003
The Pods of Deployment reporter in namespace batch stay Pending. Find the reason and fix it so that all replicas are Running. Set the memory request of the container to 128Mi. Keep the number of replicas unchanged.
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace batch --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: reporter, namespace: batch}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: reporter}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: reporter}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: reporter
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
        resources: {requests: {memory: 64Gi}}
EOF
clear

steps.title: See Pending pods
steps.why: Pending = scheduler cannot find a node.

steps.title: Read the reason
cmds: kubectl -n batch describe pod -l app=reporter | grep -A3 Events
steps.see: 0/2 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient memory, 1 node(s) had untolerated taint ...
steps.why: Events tell why a pod is not scheduled. Ignore the taint part (that is the control plane); Insufficient memory is the cause.

steps.title: Lower the request
cmds: kubectl -n batch set resources deploy reporter --requests=memory=128Mi
steps.why: Asks for less memory so a node fits.

steps.title: Check
steps.why: New pods replace the old Pending ones.

tasks.beginner: The pods ask for more memory than any node has; ask for less. Words you need: request = memory a pod reserves up front; scheduler = the part that picks a node with enough free memory; Pending = no node chosen yet.

tasks.title: CrashLoop / restarts: wrong liveness probe
tasks.question:
ssh cka01004
Deployment api in namespace web keeps restarting its Pods. Identify the cause and fix it. The nginx container listens on port 80. Do not delete the Deployment.
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace web --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: api, namespace: web}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: api}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.27-alpine
        ports: [{containerPort: 80}]
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /, port: 8080}
          initialDelaySeconds: 3
          periodSeconds: 3
          failureThreshold: 2
EOF
clear

steps.title: See restarts
steps.why: Growing RESTARTS = something kills the container.

steps.title: Read events
cmds: kubectl -n web describe pod -l app=api | grep -i -A2 liveness
steps.why: Probe checks port 8080 but nginx uses 80.

steps.title: Fix the probe port
steps.see:
In vim find these lines and change 8080 to 80:
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
then press Esc, type :wq, Enter -> deployment.apps/api edited
steps.why: Probe now checks the port nginx really uses. Edit the Deployment, not the Pod.

steps.title: Check
cmds: kubectl -n web rollout status deploy api
steps.why: The NEW pod (new name) shows RESTARTS 0 and stays healthy; the old one disappears.

tasks.docs: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes (search: livenessProbe httpGet)
tasks.beginner: The health check knocks on the wrong door (8080) so Kubernetes keeps restarting the pod. Words you need: livenessProbe = a URL the kubelet calls again and again; if it fails N times in a row the container is restarted; RESTARTS = how many times that happened.

tasks.title: Extract error lines from pod logs
tasks.question:
ssh cka01005
Pod legacy-app in namespace ops writes log lines to stdout. Write all log lines that contain the string ERROR into the file /opt/course/5/errors.txt on the controlplane node.
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace ops --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: legacy-app, namespace: ops}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","i=0; while true; do echo \"INFO tick $i\"; [ $((i%3)) -eq 0 ] && echo \"ERROR disk slow $i\"; i=$((i+1)); sleep 2; done"]
EOF
clear

steps.title: Look at the logs
steps.why: See what the lines look like.

steps.title: Save only ERROR lines
cmds: kubectl -n ops logs legacy-app | grep ERROR > /opt/course/5/errors.txt
steps.why: grep keeps only matching lines. The host you ssh'd into IS this task's controlplane. Exam: /opt needs root - if you get Permission denied, use sudo mkdir -p ... and sudo -i (Killercoda is already root).

steps.title: Check the file
steps.why: File must hold only ERROR lines.

verify: grep -vc ERROR /opt/course/5/errors.txt  # should print 0 (exit code 1 here is normal)
tasks.beginner: Copy the error lines from a pod log into a file. Words you need: stdout = what the container prints, read with kubectl logs; grep = keep only lines containing a word; > file = write the output into that file.

tasks.title: Helm: template Argo CD without CRDs
tasks.question:
ssh cka01006
Install Argo CD in the cluster using Helm:
- Add the official Argo CD Helm repository with the name argocd (https://argoproj.github.io/argo-helm).
- Generate a Helm template of the Argo CD chart version 7.7.3 for namespace argocd and save it to /root/argo-helm.yaml. Configure the chart so that it does NOT install CRDs (the CRDs are already installed in the cluster).
- Install Argo CD with Helm as release argocd, same version and configuration, in namespace argocd.
tasks.setup:
command -v helm >/dev/null || curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash
kubectl apply --server-side -k "https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/manifests/crds?ref=v2.13.2"
kubectl create namespace argocd --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
clear

steps.title: Add the repo
steps.why: Tells Helm where the chart lives.

steps.title: Find the chart and version
steps.why: Confirm the exact version exists.

steps.title: Find the CRD switch
steps.why: The chart value that controls CRDs.

steps.title: Write the template
cmds: helm template argocd argocd/argo-cd --version 7.7.3 --namespace argocd --set crds.install=false > /root/argo-helm.yaml
steps.why: template = render YAML only, nothing installed.

steps.title: Prove no CRDs inside
steps.why: Zero CRDs means the switch worked.

steps.title: Install the release
cmds: helm install argocd argocd/argo-cd --version 7.7.3 --namespace argocd --set crds.install=false
steps.why: Real install with the same settings. Pods may take 2-3 min. On the small playground some can stay Pending for lack of resources. That is OK. The release is what counts.

tasks.docs: helm.sh docs: helm template / helm install (search: helm template --set); kubernetes.io not needed
tasks.beginner: Use Helm to print Argo CD YAML into a file. Install it. Tell the chart not to add CRDs. Words you need: chart = a package of YAML templates; repo = the web address where charts live; release = one installed copy of a chart; values = the chart's settings (--set changes one); CRD = a definition that adds a new object type to Kubernetes.

tasks.title: Install cri-dockerd + kernel sysctl
tasks.question:
ssh cka01007
Prepare this node for a Docker-based container runtime:
- Install the Debian package /root/cri-dockerd.deb using dpkg.
- Enable and start the cri-docker service.
- Configure these kernel parameters so they persist across reboots (file /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf):
  net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1
  net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
  net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1
  net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 131072
tasks.setup:
test -f /root/cri-dockerd.deb || curl -fsSLo /root/cri-dockerd.deb https://github.com/Mirantis/cri-dockerd/releases/download/v0.3.16/cri-dockerd_0.3.16.3-0.ubuntu-jammy_amd64.deb || echo "download failed - check release page"
ls -l /root/cri-dockerd.deb || echo "MISSING: download a cri-dockerd .deb for your Ubuntu from https://github.com/Mirantis/cri-dockerd/releases to /root/cri-dockerd.deb"
clear

steps.title: Become root
steps.why: dpkg, systemctl and /etc need root. The real exam requires sudo -i. Killercoda is already root. If the file is missing on Killercoda, the setup download failed. Download a .deb from the cri-dockerd releases page. Or just practise the commands.

steps.title: Install the package
steps.why: dpkg installs a local .deb file. If dpkg stops with missing dependencies, run `apt-get -f install -y`. Then check again. Status `iU` means unpacked but not configured yet. `ii` means installed.

steps.title: Enable and start the service
steps.see:
Killercoda (no Docker): "Job for cri-docker.service failed" - then: enabled
Exam (Docker present): no error - then: enabled
steps.why: enable = at boot, --now = start now. Without Docker the START fails but the ENABLE still worked; is-enabled proves it.

steps.title: Write the sysctl file
cmds:
cat <<'EOF' > /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 131072
EOF
steps.why: Files in /etc/sysctl.d survive reboots. Paste the whole block at once, including the final EOF line. Everything between the two EOFs goes into the file.

steps.title: Load the kernel modules now and at every boot
steps.why: bridge-nf-call-iptables only exists when br_netfilter is loaded, nf_conntrack_max needs nf_conntrack. modprobe loads them now. The modules-load.d file loads them after a reboot. So the sysctl settings really persist.

steps.title: Apply the settings now
steps.why: Applies all /etc/sysctl.d files without rebooting.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Container Runtimes (search: cri-dockerd, sysctl ip_forward)
tasks.beginner: Install a runtime package and turn on 4 Linux network settings permanently. On Killercoda Docker is absent, so cri-docker will not start. The jammy .deb may not match a newer Ubuntu. dpkg, enable and sysctl still practise. Words you need: .deb = an Ubuntu install package (dpkg -i installs it); sysctl = a Linux kernel setting; kernel module = a driver loaded with modprobe, needed before some sysctl settings exist.

tasks.title: CRDs: list cert-manager CRDs + explain a field
tasks.question:
ssh cka01008
cert-manager CRDs are installed in the cluster.
- Create a list of all cert-manager Custom Resource Definitions and save it to /root/resources.yaml. Use kubectl's default output format; do not set an output format.
- Using kubectl, extract the documentation for the subject specification field of the Certificate custom resource and save it to /root/subject.yaml.
tasks.setup:
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.16.2/cert-manager.crds.yaml
clear

steps.title: List cert-manager CRDs
steps.why: Default output = plain table with its header, no -o flag. The label keeps only cert-manager CRDs. If it prints "No resources found", use kubectl get crd | grep cert-manager instead.

steps.title: Save the list
steps.why: Redirect the same output into the file.

steps.title: Save the field docs
steps.why: explain prints built-in docs for any field.

steps.title: Check
steps.see: GROUP: cert-manager.io  KIND: Certificate  FIELD: subject
steps.why: Confirms the right field was saved.

tasks.beginner: Show installed custom resource types in a file. Save the help text for one field. Words you need: CRD (Custom Resource Definition) = adds a new object type, like Certificate, to Kubernetes; kubectl explain = prints the built-in help for any field; default output = the normal table you get without -o.

tasks.title: RBAC: ServiceAccount, Role, RoleBinding
tasks.question:
ssh cka01009
In namespace finance create a ServiceAccount named reporter. Create a Role named pod-reader that allows only get, list and watch on pods. Bind the Role to the ServiceAccount with a RoleBinding named reporter-binding.
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace finance --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
clear

steps.title: Create the ServiceAccount
steps.why: An identity for pods/tools.

steps.title: Create the Role
steps.why: Role = list of allowed actions.

steps.title: Bind it
steps.why: Binding gives the role to the account.

steps.title: Test permissions
cmds: kubectl -n finance auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:finance:reporter
kubectl -n finance auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:finance:reporter
kubectl -n finance auth can-i watch pods --as=system:serviceaccount:finance:reporter
kubectl -n finance auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:finance:reporter
kubectl -n finance auth can-i list secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:finance:reporter
steps.why: --as = pretend to be that account. A ServiceAccount's full name is system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>. The 3 allowed verbs say yes; other verbs and other resources say no.

verify: kubectl -n finance auth can-i watch pods --as=system:serviceaccount:finance:reporter
kubectl -n finance auth can-i list secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:finance:reporter  # must be no
tasks.beginner: Give a robot account read-only access to pods in one namespace. Words you need: ServiceAccount = an identity for programs, not people; Role = a list of allowed actions (verbs) on resources in one namespace; RoleBinding = gives that Role to an account.

tasks.title: Expose container port + NodePort Service
tasks.question:
ssh cka01010
Reconfigure the existing Deployment front-end in namespace front: add a port specification named http exposing port 80/tcp of the existing container nginx.
Create a new Service named front-end-svc of type NodePort exposing the container port http, with nodePort 30080. The Service must reach the Pods of the Deployment.
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace front --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: front-end, namespace: front}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: front-end}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: front-end}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - {name: nginx, image: nginx:1.27-alpine}
EOF
clear

steps.title: Add the container port
steps.why: Names port 80 "http" on the container.

steps.title: Create the NodePort Service
steps.why: NodePort opens the same port on every node.

steps.title: Test from outside the pod network
cmds: curl -s http://$(kubectl get node node01 -o jsonpath="{.status.addresses[0].address}"):30080 | head -4
steps.why: The $(kubectl get node node01 ...) part just prints node01's IP. Node IP + 30080 reaches the pods.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Service (search: type NodePort nodePort)
tasks.beginner: Name the container port. Open it to the outside on port 30080 of every node. Words you need: containerPort = the port inside the pod (here named http); port = the Service's own port; targetPort = where the Service sends traffic (the name http works); nodePort = the port opened on every node (30000-32767).

tasks.title: Gateway API: migrate Ingress to Gateway + HTTPRoute
tasks.question:
ssh cka01011
Migrate the existing Ingress web in namespace web-app to the Gateway API, keeping HTTPS:
- Create a Gateway named web-gateway using GatewayClass nginx, with an HTTPS listener on port 443 for hostname gateway.web.example. Use the TLS Secret web-tls already referenced by the Ingress.
- Create an HTTPRoute named web-route bound to web-gateway that sends all paths (/) for gateway.web.example to Service web on port 80.
- Delete the Ingress web when done.
keys: listener HTTPS 443, host gateway.web.example, secret web-tls
delete ingress web at the end
tasks.setup:
kubectl get crd gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io >/dev/null 2>&1 || kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.2.1/standard-install.yaml
kubectl create namespace web-app --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
openssl req -x509 -nodes -newkey rsa:2048 -days 365 -subj "/CN=gateway.web.example" -keyout /tmp/web-tls.key -out /tmp/web-tls.crt 2>/dev/null
kubectl -n web-app create secret tls web-tls --cert=/tmp/web-tls.crt --key=/tmp/web-tls.key --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata: {name: nginx}
spec: {controllerName: example.net/gateway-controller}
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: web, namespace: web-app}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: web}}
    spec:
      containers: [{name: nginx, image: nginx:1.27-alpine, ports: [{containerPort: 80}]}]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: web, namespace: web-app}
spec: {selector: {app: web}, ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 80}]}
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: web, namespace: web-app}
spec:
  tls: [{hosts: [gateway.web.example], secretName: web-tls}]
  rules:
  - host: gateway.web.example
    http:
      paths:
      - {path: /, pathType: Prefix, backend: {service: {name: web, port: {number: 80}}}}
EOF
clear

steps.title: Read the Ingress you must copy
cmds: kubectl -n web-app get ingress web -o yaml | grep -A12 "^spec"
steps.why: Host, TLS secret and backend move to the new objects.

steps.title: Check the GatewayClass
steps.why: Gateway must use an existing class.

steps.title: Create the Gateway
cmds:
cat <<'EOF' > gw.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata: {name: web-gateway, namespace: web-app}
spec:
  gatewayClassName: nginx
  listeners:
  - name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
    port: 443
    hostname: gateway.web.example
    tls:
      mode: Terminate
      certificateRefs:
      - {kind: Secret, name: web-tls}
EOF
steps.why: Gateway = the entry door with TLS. Ingress host -> listener hostname. Ingress tls.secretName -> certificateRefs. Terminate = the Gateway decrypts HTTPS with that Secret.

steps.title: Create the HTTPRoute
cmds:
cat <<'EOF' > route.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: {name: web-route, namespace: web-app}
spec:
  parentRefs: [{name: web-gateway}]
  hostnames: [gateway.web.example]
  rules:
  - matches: [{path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /}}]
    backendRefs: [{name: web, port: 80}]
EOF
steps.why: Route = which traffic goes to which Service (Ingress paths/backend -> rules/backendRefs). parentRefs needs no namespace because the route is in the same namespace as the Gateway.

steps.title: Delete the old Ingress
steps.why: Migration done; old object removed.

verify: kubectl -n web-app get gateway web-gateway -o jsonpath='{.spec.listeners}'
kubectl -n web-app get httproute web-route -o yaml | grep -A6 rules
tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Gateway API (search: HTTPRoute, Gateway listener tls certificateRefs); gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io HTTPS guide
tasks.beginner: Rebuild the HTTPS Ingress as a Gateway (door + certificate). Add an HTTPRoute (path to service). No Gateway controller runs on Killercoda, so status stays Unknown - that is fine. Words you need: GatewayClass = which controller runs the Gateway; Gateway = the entry point; listener = port + protocol + hostname (+ TLS certificate); HTTPRoute = rules sending matching requests to a Service; parentRefs = the Gateway it attaches to.

tasks.title: NetworkPolicy: choose the least permissive
tasks.question:
ssh cka01012
Pods of Deployment frontend (namespace frontend) must be able to reach Pods of Deployment backend (namespace backend) on port 80. A deny-all policy already exists in namespace backend.
Review the NetworkPolicy files in /root/netpol/ and apply the ONE that allows this traffic with the least permissions. Do not delete or modify the existing policies.

steps.title: Prove traffic is blocked now
cmds: kubectl -n frontend exec deploy/frontend -- wget -qO- -T2 backend.backend
steps.why: Deny-all is in effect. backend.backend = <service>.<namespace>. If this already works, your playground's network plugin ignores NetworkPolicies. Continue anyway. The choice of file is what is graded.

steps.title: Read all three files
steps.why: Key rule: in ONE "- from" item, namespaceSelector and podSelector must BOTH match (AND). As separate items, either one is enough (OR). 1 opens everything to all pods. 3 opens all namespaces on all ports. 2 = only frontend pods from namespace frontend, only TCP 80.

steps.title: Apply the strictest correct one
steps.why: Only frontend pods, only port 80.

steps.title: Test again
cmds: kubectl -n frontend exec deploy/frontend -- wget -qO- -T2 backend.backend | head -4
steps.why: Traffic now allowed.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Network Policies (search: namespaceSelector podSelector)
tasks.beginner: Pick the rule file that opens only the needed door, nothing more. Words you need: NetworkPolicy = a firewall rule for pods; default-deny = blocks all incoming traffic to the namespace's pods; ingress from = who may connect, picked by namespace label and/or pod label.

tasks.title: PriorityClass one below the highest
tasks.question:
ssh cka01013
Create a new PriorityClass named urgent for user workloads. Its value must be exactly one less than the highest existing user-defined PriorityClass value (ignore the system-* classes).
Patch the existing Deployment busybox-logger in namespace priority to use PriorityClass urgent. Ensure the Deployment rolls out successfully.
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace priority --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata: {name: low-priority}
value: 1000
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata: {name: high-priority}
value: 5000
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: busybox-logger, namespace: priority}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: busybox-logger}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: busybox-logger}}
    spec: {containers: [{name: c, image: busybox:1.36, command: [sh, -c, "while true; do date; sleep 5; done"]}]}
EOF
clear

steps.title: List priority classes
steps.why: Highest user-defined is 5000.

steps.title: Create urgent = 4999
steps.why: One less than 5000.

steps.title: Use it in the Deployment
steps.why: Pod template now carries the class.

steps.title: Check rollout
cmds: kubectl -n priority rollout status deploy busybox-logger
steps.why: Running pod has the new priority. If you see "0 4999", the old pod is still terminating. Run it again after a few seconds.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Pod Priority and Preemption (search: PriorityClass value)
tasks.beginner: Make a new priority level just under the top one. Give it to a deployment. Words you need: PriorityClass = a named number, higher means scheduled first; preempt = push out lower-priority pods to make room; system-* classes = Kubernetes' own classes, so ignore them.

tasks.title: HPA with scale-down behavior
tasks.question:
ssh cka01014
Create a HorizontalPodAutoscaler named apache-server in namespace autoscale for the existing Deployment apache-server. It must target 50% CPU utilisation per Pod, with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 4 replicas. Set the scale-down stabilization window to 30 seconds.
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace autoscale --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: apache-server, namespace: autoscale}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: apache-server}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: apache-server}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - {name: httpd, image: httpd:2.4-alpine, resources: {requests: {cpu: 100m}}}
EOF
clear

steps.title: Create the HPA (autoscaling/v2)
cmds:
cat <<'EOF' > hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: {name: apache-server, namespace: autoscale}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: apache-server}
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 4
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: {name: cpu, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 50}}
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 30
EOF
steps.why: behavior only exists in autoscaling/v2 YAML. behavior sits directly under spec, scaleDown under behavior.

steps.title: Check it
steps.why: <unknown> = no metrics-server is installed in the playground. So there are no CPU numbers yet. The HPA object itself is still correct.

steps.title: Check the window
cmds: kubectl -n autoscale get hpa apache-server -o jsonpath="{.spec.behavior.scaleDown}"
steps.why: Proves behavior was saved. Kubernetes adds the default policies and selectPolicy itself; only the 30 matters.

verify: kubectl -n autoscale get hpa apache-server -o yaml | grep -A4 behavior
tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (search: stabilizationWindowSeconds behavior)
tasks.beginner: Auto-add pods when CPU > 50%, and wait 30 s before removing them. Words you need: HPA (HorizontalPodAutoscaler) = changes a Deployment's replica count based on load; metrics-server = the add-on that measures pod CPU for it; stabilization window = how long the HPA waits before scaling down.

tasks.title: Default StorageClass with WaitForFirstConsumer
tasks.question:
ssh cka01015
Create a StorageClass named local-fast with provisioner rancher.io/local-path and volume binding mode WaitForFirstConsumer. Make it the default StorageClass; it must be the ONLY default. Do not modify existing PersistentVolumeClaims.
tasks.setup:
kubectl get deploy -A | grep -q local-path-provisioner || kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rancher/local-path-provisioner/v0.0.30/deploy/local-path-storage.yaml
kubectl patch sc local-path -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"true"}}}'
clear

steps.title: See current classes
steps.why: "(default)" marks the current default. Note EVERY class marked (default).

steps.title: Un-default the old class first
steps.why: Remove the old default before adding the new one, so there are never two defaults. Repeat this command for each other class marked (default) in step 1. Change only the name.

steps.title: Create the new default class
cmds:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: local-fast
  annotations: {storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"}
provisioner: rancher.io/local-path
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
EOF
steps.why: The annotation (value "true" in quotes) makes it the default.

steps.title: Check
steps.why: Exactly one "(default)".

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Change the default StorageClass; Storage Classes (search: is-default-class)
tasks.beginner: Add a storage type and make it the only automatic choice. Words you need: StorageClass = a type of disk Kubernetes can create on demand; default class = the one used by a PVC that names no class; WaitForFirstConsumer = create the disk only when a pod that uses it is scheduled.

tasks.title: Reuse a retained PV for MariaDB
tasks.question:
ssh cka01016
A MariaDB Deployment in namespace mariadb was deleted by mistake, but its PersistentVolume mariadb-pv was kept.
- Create a PersistentVolumeClaim named mariadb in namespace mariadb: access mode ReadWriteOnce, storage 250Mi, so that it binds to the existing PV.
- Edit /root/mariadb-deploy.yaml so the Deployment uses this PVC, then apply it. Ensure the Pod is Running.
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace mariadb --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata: {name: mariadb-pv}
spec:
  capacity: {storage: 250Mi}
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: ""
  hostPath: {path: /mnt/data/mariadb, type: DirectoryOrCreate}
EOF
cat <<'EOF' > /root/mariadb-deploy.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: mariadb, namespace: mariadb}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: mariadb}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: mariadb}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: mariadb
        image: mariadb:11
        env: [{name: MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD, value: cka}]
        volumeMounts: [{name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/mysql}]
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: ""
EOF
clear

steps.title: Look at the PV
steps.why: Note size, mode and empty class. If STATUS is Released (common in the exam), the PV still remembers its old claim. Run kubectl patch pv mariadb-pv -p '{"spec":{"claimRef":null}}'. Then it becomes Available.

steps.title: Create the matching PVC
cmds:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: mariadb, namespace: mariadb}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: ""
  volumeName: mariadb-pv
  resources: {requests: {storage: 250Mi}}
EOF
steps.why: Empty class "" stops the default class grabbing it. volumeName: mariadb-pv guarantees it binds to exactly that PV.

steps.title: Check it is Bound
steps.why: Bound to the old PV = old data kept.

steps.title: Point the Deployment to the PVC
steps.why: sed -i 's/OLD/NEW/' file = replace text inside the file. Here claimName: "" becomes claimName: mariadb. grep shows the result before you apply.

steps.title: Check the Pod
steps.why: Database runs on the kept disk.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Configure a Pod to Use a PersistentVolume for Storage (search: PersistentVolumeClaim storageClassName)
tasks.beginner: Make a storage claim that grabs the old disk. Then plug it into the database deployment. Words you need: PV (PersistentVolume) = the disk; PVC (PersistentVolumeClaim) = a request for a disk; Bound = request matched to a disk; RWO (ReadWriteOnce) = one node can mount it read-write.

tasks.title: Kubelet fails: broken systemd drop-in
tasks.question:
ssh cka02001
Node node01 is NotReady after a maintenance change. Find out why the kubelet does not start on node01 and fix it. Do not reinstall any packages.
tasks.setup:
ssh node01 "sed -i 's#/usr/bin/kubelet #/usr/local/bin/kubelet #' /usr/lib/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf 2>/dev/null; systemctl daemon-reload; systemctl restart kubelet"
sleep 60
clear

steps.title: See the node
steps.why: Start from the symptom. If it still says Ready, wait 30 s and run it again. The grace period is ~50 s.

steps.title: Log in, become root and check kubelet
steps.why: 203/EXEC = binary path not found.

steps.title: Read the logs
steps.see: Failed at step EXEC ... /usr/local/bin/kubelet: No such file
steps.why: Logs show the wrong path.

steps.title: Find the real binary and the config
steps.see:
/usr/bin/kubelet                         (which)
ExecStart=/usr/bin/kubelet               (main unit)
ExecStart=                               (drop-in clears it)
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/kubelet $KUBELET_KUBECONFIG_ARGS ...   (drop-in)
steps.why: The LAST ExecStart wins - it points to /usr/local/bin/kubelet, which does not exist. The real binary is /usr/bin/kubelet.

steps.title: Find the drop-in file
steps.why: Each "# /path" line is a file systemd reads. Note the 10-kubeadm.conf path (it may be under /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/ instead).

steps.title: Fix the drop-in and restart
steps.see: In vim: use the path from the previous step; on the ExecStart= line change /usr/local/bin/kubelet to /usr/bin/kubelet; Esc :wq. Then: active
steps.why: daemon-reload makes systemd re-read the changed file; restart starts kubelet with the right path. Two exits: leave root, leave node01.

steps.title: Check
steps.why: Allow ~30s.

tasks.beginner: The kubelet service file points to a program path that does not exist; correct it. Words you need: unit file = systemd's recipe for starting a service; drop-in = an extra file in kubelet.service.d/ that overrides parts of the main unit; daemon-reload = tell systemd to re-read changed unit files. sudo -i = become root (needed in the exam; Killercoda is already root).

tasks.title: Scheduler down: Pods stay Pending
tasks.question:
ssh cka02002
A new Pod named stuck in namespace default stays Pending, even though nodes have free resources. Diagnose and repair the cluster component responsible so that the Pod is scheduled.
keys: fix the control plane component, not the pod
tasks.setup:
sed -i 's#^    - kube-scheduler$#    - kube-schedulerr#' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
sleep 20
kubectl run stuck --image=nginx:1.27-alpine --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
clear

steps.title: See the pod has no node
steps.why: No events at all = nobody is scheduling.

steps.title: Check the scheduler pod
cmds: kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep scheduler
steps.why: Scheduler is a static pod on controlplane.

steps.title: Read why the container cannot start
cmds: kubectl -n kube-system describe pod -l component=kube-scheduler | grep -iE 'reason|message'
steps.see:
Reason: StartError (or RunContainerError)
Message: ... exec: "kube-schedulerr": executable file not found in $PATH
steps.why: Typo in the command. crictl logs shows NOTHING here: the program never started, so it printed no log. The error is in the pod status (describe). Or check journalctl -u kubelet | grep scheduler.

steps.title: Become root and fix the static pod manifest
steps.why: Files in /etc/kubernetes/manifests need root (exam: sudo -i; Killercoda is already root). sed -i 's#OLD#NEW#' replaces text in the file. kubelet notices the change and recreates the scheduler pod by itself (~30 s).

steps.title: Check
cmds: kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep scheduler
steps.see:
kube-scheduler-controlplane 1/1 Running
stuck  1/1  Running ... <any node name>
steps.why: Pod gets a node once scheduler is back (on any node).

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Troubleshooting Clusters; Static Pods (search: /etc/kubernetes/manifests)
tasks.beginner: The scheduler program is broken by a typo in its file. Fix the file, not the pod. Words you need: scheduler = the control-plane part that picks a node for each new pod; static pod = a pod the kubelet runs from a YAML file in /etc/kubernetes/manifests; mirror pod = the read-only copy of it you see in kubectl.

tasks.title: DNS not resolving: CoreDNS down
tasks.question:
ssh cka02003
Pods can no longer resolve Service names. Fix cluster DNS so that, from Pod dns-test in namespace lookup, the name kubernetes.default resolves. Save the output of that nslookup to /root/dns.txt.
keys: fix DNS, do not edit the pod
tasks.setup:
kubectl -n kube-system scale deploy coredns --replicas=0
kubectl create namespace lookup --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n lookup run dns-test --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --dry-run=client -o yaml -- sleep 36000 | kubectl apply -f -
clear

steps.title: Try a lookup
cmds: kubectl -n lookup exec dns-test -- nslookup -timeout=2 kubernetes.default
steps.see: connection timed out; no servers could be reached
steps.why: DNS service does not answer.

steps.title: Check CoreDNS
steps.why: Somebody scaled it to zero.

steps.title: Scale it back
cmds: kubectl -n kube-system rollout status deploy coredns
steps.why: Two DNS pods again.

steps.title: Save the lookup
cmds: kubectl -n lookup exec dns-test -- nslookup kubernetes.default > /root/dns.txt; cat /root/dns.txt
steps.why: Proves DNS works. busybox also prints lines like "** server can't find kubernetes.default.cluster.local: NXDOMAIN". It tries several suffixes. It may also end with exit code 1. Ignore that. Success = a Name/Address line for kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Debugging DNS Resolution
tasks.beginner: Cluster DNS was switched off; switch it on and prove it works. Words you need: DNS = turns a name into an IP; CoreDNS = the coredns Deployment pods in kube-system that answer in-cluster name lookups; kube-dns = the Service in front of them.

tasks.title: Pending: nodeSelector matches no node
tasks.question:
ssh cka02004
Pods of Deployment analytics in namespace data are Pending. Make them run on node01 WITHOUT changing the Deployment.
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace data --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: analytics, namespace: data}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: analytics}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: analytics}}
    spec:
      nodeSelector: {disktype: ssd}
      containers: [{name: c, image: busybox:1.36, command: [sleep, "3600"]}]
EOF
clear

steps.title: Read the reason
cmds: kubectl -n data describe pod -l app=analytics | grep -A3 Events
steps.see: 0/2 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector, 1 node(s) had untolerated taint ...
steps.why: Pod wants a label no node has. The selector part is the cause; the taint part is just the control plane.

steps.title: See the required label
steps.why: This is the label to add.

steps.title: Label node01
steps.why: Now node01 matches. --overwrite = replace the value if the label already exists.

steps.title: Check
steps.why: Pending pods get scheduled automatically.

verify: kubectl get node node01 --show-labels | grep -o disktype=ssd
tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Assign Pods to Nodes (search: nodeSelector)
tasks.beginner: Pods want a node with a sticker "disktype=ssd"; put that sticker on node01. Words you need: node label = a key=value tag on a node; nodeSelector = the labels a pod demands from its node; Pending = the scheduler found no node that fits.

tasks.title: Init container blocked by missing ConfigMap
tasks.question:
ssh cka02005
Deployment inventory in namespace stock never becomes ready. Investigate and fix it. The application expects a ConfigMap named inventory-config with key ready and value yes. Do not modify the Deployment.

steps.title: See the status
steps.why: Stuck before the main container starts.

steps.title: Read events
cmds: kubectl -n stock describe pod -l app=inventory | tail -5
steps.why: The pod cannot even mount its volume. So the init container never runs. The ConfigMap behind the volume is missing.

steps.title: Create the ConfigMap
steps.why: Key "ready" becomes file /config/ready.

steps.title: Check
cmds: kubectl -n stock rollout status deploy inventory --timeout=180s
steps.why: Kubelet retries the mount with growing pauses, then the init container finds /config/ready and passes. If it times out, just run it again.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap
tasks.beginner: The pod needs a ConfigMap that was never created; create it. Words you need: ConfigMap = a key/value settings object; volume = storage mounted into the pod; ConfigMap volume = a volume that turns each key into a file; init container = a container that must finish before the main one starts.

tasks.title: Install Calico CNI with the tigera operator
tasks.question:
ssh cka02006
Install and configure a CNI of your choice that supports NetworkPolicy enforcement. Use Calico v3.29.2:
- Operator manifest: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.29.2/manifests/tigera-operator.yaml
- Custom resources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.29.2/manifests/custom-resources.yaml
The Pod CIDR must match the cluster's configured pod subnet.

steps.title: Find the cluster pod CIDR
cmds: kubectl -n kube-system get cm kubeadm-config -o yaml | grep podSubnet
steps.why: Calico must use the same range. If kubeadm-config shows no podSubnet, the second command reads it from the running kube-controller-manager. Safe to run on Killercoda.

steps.title: Install the operator (exam only)
steps.why: create, because the CRDs are too big for apply. The wait makes sure the Installation type exists before you use it. Do NOT run on Killercoda (it already has a CNI).

steps.title: Download and set the CIDR
steps.why: Download + grep are safe to practise on Killercoda. In the sed, replace 10.244.0.0/16 with YOUR podSubnet from step 1. Skip the sed if it is already 192.168.0.0/16.

steps.title: Create the Installation (exam only)
steps.why: Wait a few minutes for calico pods and for AVAILABLE True.

tasks.docs: docs.tigera.io: Quickstart for Calico on Kubernetes (kubernetes.io: Network Plugins)
tasks.beginner: Install a network plugin that understands NetworkPolicies. Killercoda already has a CNI. So DO NOT run the "exam only" steps there (setup empty). Only run step 1 and the download/grep. Rehearse the rest. Words you need: CNI = the network plugin that gives pods IPs and connects them; operator = a controller pod that installs and manages software for you; Installation = the custom object telling the Tigera operator how to set up Calico, pod CIDR included; tigerastatus = its health report.

tasks.title: etcd snapshot backup
tasks.question:
ssh cka02007
Create a snapshot of the etcd instance running at https://127.0.0.1:2379 and save it to /opt/backup/etcd-snap.db.
Use: CA /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt, cert /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt, key /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key.
tasks.setup:
command -v etcdctl >/dev/null || (apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq etcd-client)
mkdir -p /opt/backup
clear

steps.title: Become root, confirm cert paths in the etcd manifest
steps.why: /etc/kubernetes/pki and /opt/backup need root (exam: sudo -i; Killercoda is already root). export ETCDCTL_API=3 makes older etcdctl (v3.3) use the v3 API; newer ones ignore it. Never guess paths; read them.

steps.title: Take the snapshot
steps.why: Copies the whole cluster state.

steps.title: Check the file
steps.why: A table means the file is valid. A "deprecated, use etcdutl" warning is OK.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Operating etcd clusters for Kubernetes (search: snapshot save)
tasks.beginner: Save a backup copy of the cluster database into a file. Words you need: etcd = the cluster's database (every object lives there); snapshot = a one-file copy of it; CA/cert/key = the ID card etcdctl shows so etcd lets it in. On Killercoda the setup installs a distro etcdctl. It may be older than the cluster's etcd. That is fine for practice..

tasks.title: Kustomize overlay
tasks.question:
ssh cka02008
A Kustomize base exists in /root/shop-kustomize/base. Create an overlay in /root/shop-kustomize/overlays/prod that:
- uses the base,
- puts all resources in namespace shop-prod,
- adds the name prefix prod-,
- sets the replicas of Deployment shop to 3.
Apply the overlay with kubectl.
tasks.setup:
mkdir -p /root/shop-kustomize/base
cat <<'EOF' > /root/shop-kustomize/base/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: shop}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: shop}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: shop}}
    spec: {containers: [{name: shop, image: nginx:1.27-alpine}]}
EOF
cat <<'EOF' > /root/shop-kustomize/base/kustomization.yaml
resources:
- deployment.yaml
EOF
clear

steps.title: Look at the base
steps.why: Know what you are changing.

steps.title: Write the overlay
cmds:
cat <<'EOF' > /root/shop-kustomize/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
resources:
- ../../base
namespace: shop-prod
namePrefix: prod-
replicas:
- name: shop
  count: 3
EOF
steps.why: replicas uses the ORIGINAL name, without prefix.

steps.title: Preview
steps.why: Check output before applying.

steps.title: Apply
cmds: kubectl create namespace shop-prod --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
steps.why: The namespace must exist before the apply. The --dry-run | apply form also works on a re-run. Plain create would say AlreadyExists, which is harmless. -k = apply a kustomization folder.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize (search: namePrefix replicas)
tasks.beginner: Make a "prod" version of some YAML. Give it a different namespace, name prefix and replica count. Words you need: base = the original YAML folder; overlay = a folder of changes applied on top of the base; kustomization.yaml = the file that lists both; ../../base = go up two folders, then into base.

tasks.title: Helm install + upgrade with values
tasks.question:
ssh cka02009
Add the Helm repository podinfo (https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo). Install chart podinfo/podinfo version 6.7.1 as release web in namespace helm-web (create it) with 2 replicas.
Then upgrade the release, keeping the same chart version, so that the UI message is "hello cka" (value ui.message). Write the current revision number of the release to /root/helm-rev.txt.
tasks.setup:
command -v helm >/dev/null || curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash
clear

steps.title: Add the repo
steps.why: Repo = chart catalogue. A chart is an app package; installing it creates a release.

steps.title: Install
cmds: helm install web podinfo/podinfo --version 6.7.1 -n helm-web --create-namespace --set replicaCount=2
steps.why: --create-namespace makes helm-web.

steps.title: Upgrade with a new value
cmds: helm upgrade web podinfo/podinfo --version 6.7.1 -n helm-web --reuse-values --set ui.message="hello cka"
steps.why: --reuse-values keeps replicaCount=2. The question says "keeping the same chart version". So repeat --version 6.7.1. Without it, helm takes the newest chart.

steps.title: Save revision
steps.why: Take the number on the last line (deployed). > writes the output into the file (overwrites it).

tasks.docs: helm.sh docs: helm upgrade (search: --reuse-values --set)
tasks.beginner: Install an app from a Helm chart, then change one setting with an upgrade. Words you need: chart = an app package; release = one installed copy of a chart (here: web); revision = the release's version number (1 = install, +1 on every upgrade).

tasks.title: Create an Ingress with path routing
tasks.question:
ssh cka02010
Create an Ingress named echo in namespace echo-sound that exposes Service echo on port 8080 at http://example.org/echo using ingressClassName nginx and pathType Prefix.

steps.title: Check the Service port
steps.why: Ingress must use the Service port, not the pod port.

steps.title: Create the Ingress
steps.why: Format: HOST/PATH=SERVICE:PORT. The * at the end means pathType Prefix (without it: Exact).

steps.title: Check
cmds: kubectl -n echo-sound describe ingress echo | grep -A3 Rules
steps.why: Host, path and backend are right.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Ingress (search: pathType Prefix ingressClassName)
tasks.beginner: Publish a service under the web address example.org/echo. No ingress controller on Killercoda, so ADDRESS stays empty. Words you need: Ingress = web-address rules (host + path → Service:port); ingress controller = the program that really routes the traffic (none here); ingressClassName = which controller should handle the rules.

tasks.title: TLS ConfigMap: allow only TLSv1.3
tasks.question:
ssh cka02011
Deployment nginx-static in namespace nginx-static serves HTTPS using configuration from ConfigMap nginx-config. It currently allows TLSv1.2 and TLSv1.3.
Change the configuration so that ONLY TLSv1.3 is accepted, then make the ConfigMap immutable. Make sure the running Pods use the new configuration.
keys: pods must pick up the change

steps.title: Wait for nginx, then test TLS 1.2
cmds: kubectl -n nginx-static rollout status deploy nginx-static
IP=$(kubectl -n nginx-static get svc nginx-static -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'); echo $IP
steps.why: IP=$(...) stores the inner command's output in variable IP; -o jsonpath='{...}' prints one field. curl options: -s = quiet. -k = accept the self-signed cert. --tls-max 1.2 = offer at most TLS 1.2. Baseline: 1.2 is still accepted.

steps.title: Edit the ConfigMap
steps.why: vim opens the ConfigMap. Change the line to   ssl_protocols TLSv1.3;   (keep the ;), then :wq. Change content BEFORE making it immutable.

steps.title: Make it immutable
steps.why: Immutable = no more edits allowed.

steps.title: Restart the pods
cmds: kubectl -n nginx-static rollout restart deploy nginx-static && kubectl -n nginx-static rollout status deploy nginx-static
steps.why: subPath files only change on pod restart.

steps.title: Prove 1.2 is refused, 1.3 works
steps.why: curl -s prints nothing on failure; || echo refused prints 'refused' only when curl fails. Without --tls-max curl uses 1.3 and still gets ok. New shell? Set IP again (step 1).

verify: kubectl -n nginx-static get cm nginx-config -o jsonpath="{.immutable}"
kubectl -n nginx-static get cm nginx-config -o yaml | grep ssl_protocols
tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: ConfigMaps (search: immutable)
tasks.beginner: Edit nginx settings stored in a ConfigMap to allow only TLS 1.3. Lock the ConfigMap. Restart nginx. Words you need: TLS = the encryption behind https (versions 1.2, 1.3); immutable = locked, can never be edited again; subPath = mounts one file from a volume, updated only when the pod restarts.

tasks.title: Write a NetworkPolicy: namespace AND pod selector
tasks.question:
ssh cka02012
In namespace db create a NetworkPolicy named db-allow-api that allows incoming traffic to Pods labelled app=db ONLY from Pods labelled role=api in namespace api, on TCP port 80. All other incoming traffic to app=db Pods must be denied.

steps.title: Create the policy
steps.why: cat <<'EOF' > /root/np.yaml ... EOF starts a "heredoc". It writes every line up to EOF into /root/np.yaml. This is the same as pasting into vim. Same list item (no 2nd dash before podSelector) = AND. Once a policy selects app=db pods, every incoming connection it does not allow is denied.

steps.title: Check the network plugin enforces policies
steps.why: Only such plugins enforce NetworkPolicy. If none is listed, the "blocked" test will not time out. That happens even though your YAML is right.

steps.title: Allowed pod works
cmds: kubectl -n api exec api -- wget -qO- -T2 db.db | head -2
steps.why: db.db = Service db in namespace db (short DNS name service.namespace). role=api in ns api passes.

steps.title: Other pod is blocked
cmds: kubectl -n api exec web -- wget -qO- -T2 db.db
steps.why: role=web is denied.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Network Policies (search: namespaceSelector and podSelector)
tasks.beginner: Let only the api pods from the api namespace talk to the database. Allow port 80 only. Words you need: NetworkPolicy = a firewall rule for pods; ingress = incoming traffic; namespaceSelector / podSelector = pick allowed senders by namespace label / pod label.

tasks.title: Native sidecar container (restartPolicy Always)
tasks.question:
ssh cka02013
Update Deployment order-app in namespace logging: add a sidecar container named log-shipper using image busybox:1.36 that runs: tail -n+1 -F /var/log/order.log
Use the native sidecar pattern (an init container with restartPolicy: Always). Share the log directory using a volume named logs mounted at /var/log in both containers. Do not change the existing container's command.
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace logging --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: order-app, namespace: logging}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: order-app}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: order-app}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: [sh, -c, "while true; do echo order $(date) >> /var/log/order.log; sleep 3; done"]
EOF
clear

steps.title: Save the current YAML
cmds: kubectl -n logging get deploy order-app -o yaml > /root/order-app.yaml
steps.why: Backup before big edits (restore with kubectl replace --force -f /root/order-app.yaml).

steps.title: Add the sidecar with kubectl edit
steps.why:
vim opens the live Deployment. Under spec.template.spec, add initContainers and volumes. Add volumeMounts to the existing app container. Do not touch its command. Spaces matter:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: log-shipper
        image: busybox:1.36
        restartPolicy: Always
        command: [sh, -c, "tail -n+1 -F /var/log/order.log"]
        volumeMounts:
        - {name: logs, mountPath: /var/log}
      containers:
      - name: app
        ...existing lines stay...
        volumeMounts:
        - {name: logs, mountPath: /var/log}
      volumes:
      - {name: logs, emptyDir: {}}
Save with :wq. If vim reopens with an error at the top, fix the indentation and save again. restartPolicy Always turns the init container into a sidecar.

steps.title: Check both run
steps.why: Sidecar counts as a running container.

steps.title: Read sidecar logs
steps.why: Sidecar sees the app log file. (Mounting at /var/log hides busybox's own empty /var/log - harmless.)

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Sidecar Containers (search: initContainers restartPolicy Always)
tasks.beginner: Add a helper container that keeps reading the app log file through a shared folder. Native sidecars are stable since v1.33. Words you need: init container = runs before the app starts; native sidecar = an init container with restartPolicy: Always, running beside the app; emptyDir = an empty shared folder that lives as long as the Pod.

tasks.title: Split node resources evenly across replicas
tasks.question:
ssh cka02014
Deployment wordpress in namespace wp runs 3 replicas on node01 (it has an init container). Its Pods stay Pending.
Scale the Deployment to 0. Then give each Pod an equal share of node01's remaining CPU and memory: take node01's allocatable minus what is already requested by other Pods, keep 10% as headroom, and divide the rest by 3. Use identical requests for the init container and the main container. Scale back to 3 and ensure all Pods are Running.

steps.title: See why the Pods are Pending
cmds: kubectl -n wp describe pod -l app=wordpress | grep -m1 Insufficient
steps.see: Pending ... / FailedScheduling ... Insufficient cpu, Insufficient memory
steps.why: A Pod needs max(biggest init container, sum of main containers). The init container asks 4 CPU / 8Gi - more than node01 has. So no Pod fits, even though the main container is small.

steps.title: Scale to 0
steps.why: Its own requests must not count while you calculate.

steps.title: Read node01 numbers
cmds: kubectl describe node node01 | grep -A7 Allocatable
kubectl describe node node01 | grep -A6 "Allocated resources"
steps.see:
Allocatable: cpu: 1  memory: 1928288Ki (example)
Allocated: Resource Requests Limits / cpu 250m (25%) ... / memory 150Mi (7%) ...
steps.why: Allocatable = what pods may use. In "Allocated resources" take the Requests column (first number), not Limits. cpu 1 = 1000m (cpu 2 = 2000m). Memory is in Ki: Ki ÷ 1024 = Mi. Your numbers will differ - write them down.

steps.title: Calculate with real arithmetic
steps.why: $(( ... )) = shell integer arithmetic (it always rounds down). Put YOUR numbers in. Allocatable memory Ki ÷ 1024 = Mi. (allocatable - requested) × 90 / 100 keeps 10% headroom. Then / 3 = one Pod's share.

steps.title: Set requests on both containers
cmds: kubectl -n wp set resources deploy wordpress -c init --requests=cpu=225m,memory=519Mi
kubectl -n wp set resources deploy wordpress -c wordpress --requests=cpu=225m,memory=519Mi
steps.why: -c picks the container (the init container too). Use YOUR results from the step before.

steps.title: Scale back and check
steps.why: All three fit now.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Resource Management for Pods and Containers (search: requests init containers)
tasks.beginner: Share what is free on node01 fairly between 3 pods so all of them fit. Words you need: requests = the CPU/memory the scheduler reserves for a container; Allocatable = what node01 can give to pods; 1000m (millicores) = 1 CPU, and 1024Ki = 1Mi.

tasks.title: PVC Pending: wrong StorageClass
tasks.question:
ssh cka02015
PVC logs-pvc in namespace storage-fix stays Pending and Pod log-writer cannot start. Fix it so the PVC is Bound using StorageClass local-path (same name, size 200Mi, ReadWriteOnce) and the Pod is Running.
tasks.setup:
kubectl get deploy -A | grep -q local-path-provisioner || kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rancher/local-path-provisioner/v0.0.30/deploy/local-path-storage.yaml
kubectl create namespace storage-fix --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: logs-pvc, namespace: storage-fix}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: fast-ssd
  resources: {requests: {storage: 200Mi}}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: log-writer, namespace: storage-fix}
spec:
  containers:
  - {name: c, image: busybox:1.36, command: [sh, -c, "while true; do date >> /data/log; sleep 5; done"], volumeMounts: [{name: d, mountPath: /data}]}
  volumes: [{name: d, persistentVolumeClaim: {claimName: logs-pvc}}]
EOF
clear

steps.title: Read the reason
cmds: kubectl -n storage-fix describe pvc logs-pvc | tail -3
steps.why: The class does not exist. local-path uses WaitForFirstConsumer. It creates the disk only when a Pod uses the claim. So even a correct PVC shows Pending until its Pod exists.

steps.title: Save the Pod, then delete Pod and PVC
cmds: kubectl -n storage-fix get pod log-writer -o yaml > /root/log-writer.yaml
steps.why: storageClassName cannot be edited on a PVC, so it must be recreated. The Pod goes first. A PVC used by a Pod is not removed. Save the Pod first so you can bring it back unchanged. A plain delete is enough for a Pending pod.

steps.title: Create the fixed PVC
cmds:
cat <<'EOF' > /root/logs-pvc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: logs-pvc, namespace: storage-fix}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: local-path
  resources: {requests: {storage: 200Mi}}
EOF
steps.why: cat <<'EOF' > /root/logs-pvc.yaml ... EOF starts a "heredoc". It writes every line up to EOF into /root/logs-pvc.yaml. This is the same as pasting into vim. Same name, size and mode; right class.

steps.title: Recreate the Pod from the saved file
steps.why: A saved object still carries resourceVersion. The API refuses to create an object that has one. The error says "resourceVersion should not be set on objects to be created". sed deletes that line (and uid). status and creationTimestamp are simply ignored.

steps.title: Check
steps.see: logs-pvc Bound ... local-path / log-writer 1/1 Running (can take ~30 s)
steps.why: local-path binds when the pod starts.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Persistent Volumes (search: storageClassName Pending)
tasks.beginner: The storage request names a storage type that does not exist. Recreate it with the right type. Words you need: PVC = a request for a disk; StorageClass = the kind of disk and who creates it (here local-path); WaitForFirstConsumer = the disk is made only when a Pod uses the claim.

tasks.title: Static PV + PVC + Pod (hostPath)
tasks.question:
ssh cka02016
Create a PersistentVolume app-pv: 1Gi, ReadWriteOnce, hostPath /srv/app-data, storageClassName manual.
Create a PersistentVolumeClaim app-pvc in namespace app-store requesting 500Mi from class manual.
Create a Pod app-writer (image busybox:1.36, command sleep 3600) in namespace app-store mounting the claim at /data.
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace app-store --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
clear

steps.title: Create PV, PVC and Pod
cmds:
cat <<'EOF' > /root/all.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata: {name: app-pv}
spec:
  capacity: {storage: 1Gi}
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: manual
  hostPath: {path: /srv/app-data}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: app-pvc, namespace: app-store}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: manual
  resources: {requests: {storage: 500Mi}}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: app-writer, namespace: app-store}
spec:
  containers:
  - {name: c, image: busybox:1.36, command: [sleep, "3600"], volumeMounts: [{name: d, mountPath: /data}]}
  volumes: [{name: d, persistentVolumeClaim: {claimName: app-pvc}}]
EOF
steps.see: persistentvolume/app-pv created, persistentvolumeclaim/app-pvc created, pod/app-writer created
steps.why: cat <<'EOF' > /root/all.yaml ... EOF starts a "heredoc". It writes every line up to EOF into /root/all.yaml. This is the same as pasting into vim. --- separates objects in one file. PV = disk, PVC = request, Pod = user.

steps.title: Check binding
cmds: kubectl get pv app-pv; kubectl -n app-store get pvc,pod
steps.why: The PVC gets the 1Gi PV (bigger is OK). So the PVC also shows CAPACITY 1Gi, the PV's size.

steps.title: Write a test file
cmds: kubectl -n app-store exec app-writer -- sh -c "echo hi > /data/t && cat /data/t"
steps.why: Proves the mount is writable.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Configure a Pod to Use a PersistentVolume for Storage
tasks.beginner: Make a disk, request it, and mount it into a pod. Words you need: PV = a piece of storage; PVC = a request that binds to a matching PV; hostPath = a folder on the node where the Pod runs (here usually node01).

tasks.title: API server down after etcd change
tasks.question:
ssh cka03001
After a migration, kubectl on the controlplane can no longer reach the cluster ("connection refused"). The kube-apiserver is configured incorrectly. Find the problem and repair the cluster. Do not restore any backup.
keys: etcd client port is 2379 (peer port is 2380)
tasks.setup:
sed -i "s#--etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2379#--etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2380#" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
sleep 30
clear

steps.title: See the symptom
steps.why: sudo -i = become root. It is needed for node files. On Killercoda you already are root, so it is harmless. The kubectl error IS the symptom: the API server is down, so use crictl instead.

steps.title: Find the apiserver container
steps.see: kube-apiserver Exited, or Running/Created with the ATTEMPT count rising
steps.why: kubelet keeps restarting it. crictl talks to the container runtime directly, without the API server.

steps.title: Read its logs
cmds: crictl logs $(crictl ps -a --name kube-apiserver -q | head -1) 2>&1 | tail -5
steps.why: $(...) runs the inner command (finds the container ID) and pastes its output in place. 2>&1 also shows error output. It talks to the etcd PEER port.

steps.title: Compare with etcd
steps.why: 2379 is for clients like the apiserver.

steps.title: Fix the manifest
steps.why: kubelet notices the change and restarts the pod.

steps.title: Wait and check
steps.why: Press Ctrl+C to leave watch once the line shows Running. Takes ~1 minute.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Troubleshooting Clusters (search: crictl logs static pod)
tasks.beginner: The API server dials the wrong etcd port; change 2380 back to 2379. Words you need: static pod = a pod kubelet runs from a /etc/kubernetes/manifests file, restarted when edited; etcd = the cluster database; 2379 = etcd client port (for the API server), 2380 = peer port (etcd-to-etcd).

tasks.title: Controller-manager broken: Deployment does not scale
tasks.question:
ssh cka03002
Deployment scale-test in namespace cm-test was scaled to 3 replicas, but only 1 Pod exists and no new ReplicaSet activity happens. Find the responsible control plane component and fix it.
keys: fix the component, not the deployment
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace cm-test --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n cm-test create deployment scale-test --image=nginx:1.27-alpine --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
sleep 5
sed -i "s#--kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.conf#--kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.cfg#" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml
sleep 20
kubectl -n cm-test scale deploy scale-test --replicas=3
clear

steps.title: See the symptom
steps.why: Nothing creates the missing pods.

steps.title: Check the controller-manager
cmds: kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep controller-manager
steps.why: Controllers create pods for Deployments.

steps.title: Read logs
steps.why: Wrong kubeconfig file name.

steps.title: Find and fix the flag
steps.why: sudo -i = become root. It is needed for node files. On Killercoda you already are root, so it is harmless. The flag names a file that does not exist. *.conf = every name ending in .conf. Point it to the real one. kubelet restarts the static pod by itself.

steps.title: Check
steps.see: READY 3/3 (after ~1 min; repeat the command until it shows)
steps.why: The controller-manager restarts, then catches up automatically.

verify: kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep controller-manager
tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: kube-controller-manager; Troubleshooting Clusters
tasks.beginner: The program that creates pods for deployments has a wrong file path; correct it. Words you need: controller-manager = the control-plane program whose loops create Pods for Deployments/ReplicaSets; kubeconfig = the login file a component uses to talk to the API server.

tasks.title: Kubelet config: wrong client CA file
tasks.question:
ssh cka03003
node01 is NotReady. The kubelet service fails to start. Repair the kubelet configuration on node01 so that the node becomes Ready. Do not re-join the node.
tasks.setup:
ssh node01 "sed -i 's#clientCAFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt#clientCAFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca-wrong.crt#' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml; systemctl restart kubelet"
sleep 45
clear

steps.title: Log in and check status
steps.why: sudo -i = become root. It is needed for node files. On Killercoda you already are root, so it is harmless. kubelet starts then crashes.

steps.title: Read the error
steps.see: ... unable to load client CA file /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca-wrong.crt ...
steps.why: -n 30 = only the newest 30 log lines (old boot errors would mislead). The file does not exist.

steps.title: Find the right file
steps.see: ls shows ca.crt (no ca-wrong.crt); grep shows clientCAFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca-wrong.crt
steps.why: Worker nodes have only ca.crt.

steps.title: Fix and restart
steps.why: kubelet reads config.yaml at start.

steps.title: Back to controlplane and check
steps.why: First exit leaves root, second leaves node01. Allow ~30s.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Set Kubelet Parameters Via A Configuration File
tasks.beginner: The kubelet settings file names a certificate that does not exist; fix the name. Words you need: kubelet = the agent on each node that runs the pods; client CA file = the certificate kubelet uses to trust callers; NotReady = the node's kubelet is not reporting healthy.

tasks.title: NetworkPolicy blocks DNS egress
tasks.question:
ssh cka03004
In namespace secure, Pod client can reach Service backend by IP but not by name. Existing NetworkPolicies must stay unchanged. Create an additional NetworkPolicy named allow-dns in namespace secure that allows all Pods in the namespace to send DNS queries (UDP and TCP 53) to the cluster DNS Pods in kube-system.

steps.title: Name fails, IP works
cmds: kubectl -n secure exec client -- wget -qO- -T2 backend
kubectl -n secure exec client -- wget -qO- -T2 $(kubectl -n secure get pod backend -o jsonpath="{.status.podIP}") | head -2
steps.why: The first wget takes a few seconds before "bad address". $(...) pastes the pod IP printed by the inner command (jsonpath prints one field). Classic sign: DNS (port 53) is blocked.

steps.title: Check DNS pod labels
steps.why: Target for the new rule.

steps.title: Create allow-dns
steps.why: cat <<'EOF' > /root/dns.yaml ... EOF starts a "heredoc". It writes every line up to EOF into /root/dns.yaml. This is the same as pasting into vim. podSelector: {} = every pod in the namespace. Policies add up; this one opens only DNS.

steps.title: Test by name
cmds: kubectl -n secure exec client -- wget -qO- -T3 backend | head -2
steps.why: Name resolves and connects.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Network Policies (search: egress port 53)
tasks.beginner: A firewall rule blocks name lookups; add a rule that allows DNS only. Words you need: egress = outgoing traffic; default-deny-egress blocks everything going out, DNS too; DNS = turns a name like backend into an IP (CoreDNS pods, label k8s-app=kube-dns).

tasks.title: Bad rollout: roll back and record image
tasks.question:
ssh cka03005
A recent update of Deployment checkout in namespace release is broken: its new Pods cannot start. Roll the Deployment back to the last working revision. Then write the image used by the running Pods to /root/checkout-image.txt.
tasks.setup:
kubectl create namespace release --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n release create deployment checkout --image=nginx:1.27-alpine --replicas=2 --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n release rollout status deploy checkout --timeout=90s
kubectl -n release set image deploy/checkout nginx=nginx:1.27-doesnotexist
clear

steps.title: See the problem
steps.why: New image tag does not exist.

steps.title: See history
cmds: kubectl -n release rollout history deploy checkout
kubectl -n release rollout history deploy checkout --revision=1 | grep Image
steps.why: --revision=1 shows that revision's image: the working one.

steps.title: Roll back
cmds: kubectl -n release rollout undo deploy checkout
kubectl -n release rollout status deploy checkout
steps.why: undo = go to previous revision.

steps.title: Save the image
steps.why: jsonpath prints one field; > writes it into the file. The last command reads the image from the pods themselves.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Deployments (search: rollout undo)
tasks.beginner: An update broke the app; undo it and note which image works. Words you need: rollout = a Deployment update; revision = a numbered version of the Pod template; ImagePullBackOff = the image cannot be downloaded.

tasks.title: cri-dockerd + sysctl (persist + verify)
tasks.question:
ssh cka03006
Set up cri-dockerd on this node:
- Install /root/cri-dockerd.deb with dpkg.
- Enable and start the cri-docker socket and service so they start on boot.
- Persist these kernel settings in /etc/sysctl.d/99-cri.conf and load them now:
  net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1, net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1, net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1, net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 131072
- Make sure the br_netfilter module is loaded at boot (/etc/modules-load.d/cri.conf).
tasks.setup:
test -f /root/cri-dockerd.deb || curl -fsSLo /root/cri-dockerd.deb https://github.com/Mirantis/cri-dockerd/releases/download/v0.3.16/cri-dockerd_0.3.16.3-0.ubuntu-jammy_amd64.deb || echo "download failed - get cri-dockerd_0.3.16.3-0.ubuntu-jammy_amd64.deb from https://github.com/Mirantis/cri-dockerd/releases/tag/v0.3.16 and save it as /root/cri-dockerd.deb"
clear

steps.title: Install
steps.see: Setting up cri-dockerd ... (on Killercoda it may stop with dependency errors - note them and continue)
steps.why: sudo -i = become root. It is needed for node files. On Killercoda you already are root, so it is harmless. dpkg -i installs a local .deb package.

steps.title: Enable socket and service
steps.see:
enabled
enabled   ("Job for cri-docker.service failed" is expected here: no Docker. Enabled is what counts.)
steps.why: Both units start on boot.

steps.title: Module at boot
steps.why: br_netfilter lets iptables see bridged pod traffic; the bridge sysctl needs it. File in modules-load.d = load at boot; modprobe = load now.

steps.title: Persist sysctl
cmds:
cat <<'EOF' > /etc/sysctl.d/99-cri.conf

net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1

EOF
steps.why: cat <<'EOF' > /etc/sysctl.d/99-cri.conf ... EOF starts a "heredoc". It writes every line up to EOF into /etc/sysctl.d/99-cri.conf. This is the same as pasting into vim. One setting per line.

steps.title: Load and verify
steps.why: Values active now and after reboot.

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Container Runtimes (search: Forwarding IPv4 and letting iptables see bridged traffic)
tasks.beginner: Install a runtime package and make it start at boot. Set 4 kernel network switches permanently. Docker is absent on Killercoda. So the service may fail to stay active. The rest still practises. Words you need: sysctl = a kernel setting; kernel module = a driver loaded into Linux (br_netfilter); socket unit = systemd listens and starts the service when something connects.

tasks.title: Helm template Argo CD and apply with kubectl
tasks.question:
ssh cka03007
Using the Helm repository argocd (https://argoproj.github.io/argo-helm), render chart argo-cd version 7.7.3 as release argo for namespace gitops:
- CRDs must NOT be part of the output (they are pre-installed).
- The argocd-server Service must be of type NodePort.
Save the rendered manifests to /root/argocd-template.yaml and deploy them with kubectl (not helm install) into namespace gitops.
tasks.setup:
command -v helm >/dev/null || curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash
kubectl apply --server-side -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v2.13.2/manifests/crds/application-crd.yaml -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v2.13.2/manifests/crds/applicationset-crd.yaml -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v2.13.2/manifests/crds/appproject-crd.yaml
clear

steps.title: Add repo
steps.why: Repo = chart catalogue; argo-helm hosts the argo-cd chart.

steps.title: Find value names
steps.see:
crds: ... install: true
  service: ... type: ClusterIP   (inside server:)
steps.why: Look up keys, never guess. sed -n '/^server:/,/^[a-z]/p' prints only the server: section. It stops at the next top-level key. So grep finds server.service, not the dex/redis services. Or open the file in vim and search /^server:

steps.title: Render
cmds: helm template argo argocd/argo-cd --version 7.7.3 --namespace gitops --set crds.install=false --set server.service.type=NodePort > /root/argocd-template.yaml
steps.why: helm template only PRINTS the YAML. Nothing goes to the cluster. helm install would deploy it and track a release. > saves it into the file.

steps.title: Check content
steps.why: Both requirements visible in the file.

steps.title: Apply with kubectl
steps.why: kubectl applies the rendered YAML. Name = release (argo) + the chart's name argocd + -server.

steps.title: Wait for the pods
steps.why: Argo CD is big for a playground. ContainerCreating/Pending for a few minutes is a resource limit. It is not your mistake.

tasks.docs: helm.sh docs: helm template (search: --set --namespace)
tasks.beginner: Print Argo CD YAML with Helm using two settings. Save it, then apply it with kubectl. Words you need: Helm chart = an app package with settings (values); helm template = render to YAML only, helm install = render and deploy; CRD = adds a new object kind to Kubernetes (pre-installed here).

tasks.title: CRDs: filter by group + create a custom resource
tasks.question:
ssh cka03008
cert-manager CRDs are installed.
- Write the names of all CRDs belonging to API group cert-manager.io, one per line and sorted, to /root/cm-crds.txt.
- Create a ClusterIssuer named selfsigned with apiVersion cert-manager.io/v1 that uses the selfSigned issuer type.

steps.why: custom-columns prints two columns, NAME and GROUP. awk '$2=="cert-manager.io"{print $1}' keeps rows whose 2nd column is exactly cert-manager.io. It prints the 1st column. sort orders them. > saves. acme.cert-manager.io items are a different group.

steps.title: Check the kind exists

steps.title: Save the field docs

tasks.docs: kubernetes.io: Extend the Kubernetes API with CustomResourceDefinitions
